newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Soldiers plan protests as PNG's Chan faces censure.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers plan protests as PNG's Chan faces censure.

text.p: Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan came under mounting pressure to quit on Tuesday as rebel soldiers threatened to join street protests against him for the first time since crisis gripped the country last week.

A senior army officer said about 80 unarmed soldiers had been authorised to leave Port Moresby's Murray Barracks -- where they have been holed up for eight days -- to join an anti-Chan protest march on parliament.
Other soldiers, some of them lightly-armed, could be seen escorting student demonstrators to a sit-in outside parliament and driving the leaders of an angry civilian protest.
Parliament was to start sitting at 2 p.m. (0400 GMT), when Chan faced an opposition censure motion over his hiring of foreign mercenaries to crush an island uprising.
The resolution is non-binding but would further increase pressure on Chan to step down.
The mercenaries were expelled from PNG last week after an army revolt.
A senior army officer, chief of staff Alfred Renagi, said 80 soldiers would march on parliament but would spend only 10-15 minutes there in a peaceful token protest.
"We are doing this as a show of support for our cause," Renagi told Reuters. "But we do not want the public to join us."
Small numbers of other soldiers were visible on the streets.
A group of 1,000 student protesters received an army escort and the leaders of another civilian protest were being driven around by soldiers in a government light truck.
Riot police reinforcements were called in but the protesters -- chanting "people's power" -- were let through police roadblocks set up to prevent unrest.
"There's no fucking police, there's no fucking law, we are taking over," some of the protesters shouted.
Support for Chan was further eroded on Monday when five ministers, including three from his own party, said they were resigning and that more would follow.

The crisis, the worst in Papua New Guinea's 22 years of independence, began a week ago when army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok turned against Chan and demanded that he terminate the mercenary contract and quit.
Chan sacked the general and tried to ride out the storm but Singirok, popular with his troops, remains in effective control of the army as violent protests increased pressure on Chan.
Opposition politicians and resigning ministers appeared on local radio on Tuesday morning urging calm, but repeating their calls for Chan to step down.

Chief Emeka Anyaoku, the Commonwealth secretary-general, arrived in Port Moresby late on Monday on a mediation mission and went to meet the rebel army leaders at Murray Barracks shortly before the soldiers were due to march.
Opposition leader Roy Yaki said the country had been forced into a "serious crisis".
"We as members of parliament have been very clearly put to a special task to ensure that within our abilities we save this nation from total chaos and bloodshed," he said.
He called for a caretaker government to be appointed until national elections, due in June.

"The question is not a question of alternative government," Yaki said. "The question is whether it is in the interest of Papua New Guinea that he (Chan) should continue as prime minister of this country."
Michael Somare, the country's first prime minister and regarded as the father of the nation, appealed for calm and for people to obey the law.
"I am appealing for Papua New Guinea's people to stay cool, calm and allow the normal democratic process to take its course," Somare said.
Former agriculture minister David Mai, who resigned on Monday, said the abortive mercenary deal with Sandline International had never been discussed in cabinet and was unconstitutional.
"Cabinet never endorsed the Sandline deal. Therefore in my view it is unconstitutional," he said.
Mai said he expected more cabinet ministers to quit and to call on Chan, his deputy Chris Haiveta and defence minister Mathias Ijape, to step down.
The eight-day crisis has preoccupied Papua New Guinea's Pacific neighbours.

Australia, PNG's former colonial power, has had troops on standby to help around 10,000 Australian nationals who live in the country if the situation deteriorates and New Zealand has also been drawing up contingency plans.
